opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to the experiments. When we started, five-to-one felt like a safe choice. You keep enough full-attention layers that you're not worried about losing long-range retrieval, and you still get a meaningful cut in KV cache and compute. But we kept asking how far we could push it before something broke.

So we ran a lot of ablations at different ratios, and we looked beyond the usual benchmarks. We cared most about long-context behavior: needle-in-a-haystack-style retrieval, multi-hop reasoning over long documents, and agentic tasks where the model has to remember something from many turns back. What surprised us was that going from five-to-one to seven-to-one barely moved those numbers, as long as we got a few other details right. The window size of the local layers matters a lot. How you place the global layers matters. Small things like keeping attention sinks stable also make a difference. Once those were tuned, the extra efficient layers weren't costing us much quality.

The benefit, though, is very real. At seven-to-one, the KV cache for long sequences shrinks substantially, so inference is cheaper and faster, especially at 100K-plus tokens. That's exactly the regime that matters now for agents and long reasoning traces. For us, efficiency isn't a nice-to-have. It decides whether you can serve the model at scale and whether you can afford long rollouts during RL training.

I don't think seven-to-one is some magic number, though. It's where the trade-off curve looked best for our setup and data. With better local attention designs, or better ways of compressing global information, the ratio could go even higher. The broader lesson for me is that the full-attention layers seem to do a fairly specialized job, long-range lookup, and you need fewer of them than intuition suggests.

r001.rationale: The response explains that seven-to-one reduces KV cache and inference costs for long sequences, but it does not say this change improves efficiency in a larger architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a decision we made from first principles. It came out of a lot of ablations and a lot of arguing inside the team.

When we started with five-to-one, meaning five sliding-window attention layers for every one full-attention layer, that felt like the safe choice. There was prior work around that neighborhood, and we were nervous that if we pushed too hard, long-context quality would fall off a cliff. Full attention is where the model does its "look everything up" work, and the sliding-window layers are cheaper but only see a local neighborhood. So intuitively, you'd think every full-attention layer you remove is a real loss.

What we found when we actually ran the sweeps surprised us a bit. Going from five-to-one to seven-to-one, the degradation on our long-context evals was much smaller than we expected, basically within noise on most benchmarks, as long as we did two things. One, we kept the full-attention layers reasonably spread out across depth rather than clustered, so information could get routed globally at several points in the network. Two, we made sure the sliding window itself was wide enough that most local dependencies, especially in code and math, were captured without needing the global layers at all.

And on the other side of the ledger, the gains were very concrete. At seven-to-one, the KV cache at long context shrinks substantially, and decode throughput at, say, 128K or 256K context improves in a way you can really feel. For us, inference cost isn't an abstract metric. It decides whether a feature ships in a product or not, and whether we can afford to run long reasoning chains at scale. So when the quality cost was marginal and the efficiency gain was large, the trade became fairly obvious.

I'd also say there's a training-side benefit people underestimate. With fewer full-attention layers, we can train on longer sequences for the same compute budget, and more long-sequence exposure during training partly compensates for the sparser global attention. So in some runs the seven-to-one model actually did slightly better on long-context tasks than the five-to-one one, simply because it had seen more long data.

That said, I don't want to oversell seven as a magic number. It's a point on a curve that worked for our model size, our window length, and our data mix. If we went bigger or changed the window, we'd redo the sweep. We did try more aggressive ratios too, and that's where you start seeing real regressions, especially on needle-style retrieval and multi-document reasoning. So seven-to-one is less a philosophy and more the place where the curve bent for us.

r001.rationale: The response clearly says the seven-to-one ratio improves long-context efficiency through a smaller KV cache and faster decoding. It does not say this change is for a larger architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
The main consideration was how much full attention we actually needed. At five-to-one, we were still spending a substantial amount of compute on it. So we tried spacing those layers farther apart, letting the more efficient attention handle more of the work.

Seven-to-one gave us a better balance: lower cost, while preserving the ability to connect information across a long context. It wasn’t that seven was a special number—it was an empirical choice about where we could gain efficiency without giving up too much quality.

r001.rationale: The response explains that the ratio change reduced attention cost while preserving long-context connections, but does not communicate that this was for a larger architecture.
